                          COMMENTS OF LANCIUM LLC ON
                      STAFF'S RECOMMENDED ADOPTION ORDER

Introduction
Lancium LLC appreciates the Commission's and Staffs work to implement Senate Bill 6 and
establish consistent large load interconnection standards. These comments address Staffs
September 3,2026 recommended adoption order for consideration at the September 11 Open
Meeting.1 We support protecting ratepayers from stranded infrastructure costs while preserving
a predictable path for project development in Texas. Two implementation issues warrant further
clarity, particularly for projects approaching energization in Q4 2026 and beyond.
Executive Summary
• Establish and publish firm dates for adoption and implementation of the Standard Large Load
  Interconnection Agreement (SLLIA), with a transition process that allows otherwise eligible
  Batch Zero base loads to energize without delay attributable to the form's availability.
• Coordinate Project No. 58000 and the SLLIA proceeding to recognize prior payments and
   security, address the circumstances of substantially completed projects, and prevent
   duplicative collateral for the same costs and exposure.
SLLIA Timing and the Transition for Base Loads
For qualifying Batch Zero loads unenergized when the rule takes effect, recommended
§25.194(h)(3) requires execution of a SLLIA, while subsection (f) ties the execution deadline to
ERCOT's issuance of a capacity-allocation study report. The recommended order leaves
adoption of the standard form to a future proceeding. This creates uncertainty for base loads
that are not subject to additional Batch Zero study and could otherwise be ready to energize
before that study is completed, subject to ERCOT's verification and applicable energization
requirements.2
We respectfully request Commissioners direct staff to publish an implementation schedule
identifying firm dates for SLLIA adoption, availability for execution, and transition from existing
agreements. The Commission should also clarify the execution deadline applicable to these
base loads and provide an interim agreement or other transition mechanism if the standard form

 is unavailable when a project is otherwise eligible to energize. A dependable schedule will
support financing decisions and avoid additional uncertainty for lenders and investors
supporting projects already under construction or nearing completion.
Financial Security and Recognition of Existing Commitments
Recommended §25.194(f)(2)(B) requires security equal to the greater of $50,000 per MW of
contracted peak demand or allocated system-upgrade costs, and permits additional security
related to minimum billing demand. We appreciate the provisions for returning or crediting
existing security and the limited protection for direct interconnection costs under agreements
executed on or before June 1, 2025.3 Even with these protections, the resulting requirements
may create substantial incremental commitments late in development.
For projects with completed studies and agreements executed before SB 6's enactment,
substantially completed construction, and satisfied interconnection payment and upgrade-
security obligations, implementation should account for the significant commitments already
made. In the SLLIA proceeding and Project No. 58000, the Commission should specify how
applicable credits and replacement collateral will be coordinated and identify the remaining
exposure that any incremental security is intended to cover.
Those proceedings should also prevent overlapping collateral to the extent "system upgrade"
security and any minimum billing demand security cover the same infrastructure costs and risk.
Where those costs have already been fully paid or secured, a second collateral requirement for
the same exposure provides no additional stranded-cost protection. Any additional requirement
should be supported by a distinct, uncovered obligation, with clear crediting and release
provisions. This approach would preserve ratepayer protections while improving certainty
regarding the total financial commitment required to complete and operate a project. "System
upgrade" payments that cover the same costs as the minimum billing demand would be
duplicative.
Conclusion
We appreciate the opportunity to offer these implementation recommendations and request
coordinated guidance in the SLLIA proceeding and Project No. 58000 to support timely
energization and continued investment in Texas.
Respectfully submitted,


Evan Neel
Sr. Director, Regulatory and Power Services
Lancium LLC
